name: Health & Emergencies
description: Doctor, pharmacy, the body and emergency phrases for when it matters (English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese).

entries.notes: A medicinal drug or treatment, not the field of study.
The illness, not the temperature.
A skin injury from heat, not a fire or verb.
A doctor's written order for medicine, not a recipe or general instruction.
Sensation of spinning or disorientation, not foolish.
A scheduled meeting with a professional, not a decorative or casual arrangement.
Sleep or relaxation as recovery, not a remainder or pause.
Fingernail or toenail, not a metal fastener.
A small adhesive plaster for minor cuts, not a full bandage.
Harmless; often of tumours that are not cancer.
A small container holding medicine, not a spacecraft or protective covering.
A routine medical examination, not inspection or verification in other contexts.
A pad applied to the skin for treatment, not to squeeze something smaller.
A head injury from impact, causing temporary brain disruption.
Buildup of fluid or traffic; blocked passages (nasal, traffic, etc.).
Sudden involuntary muscle tightening, not a confined space.
The healing process or recovery from illness, not a treatment method.
A fluid-filled sac that grows abnormally in the body.
Spinning sensation or loss of balance, often brief and recoverable.
Intravenous fluid delivery system, not liquid falling drop by drop.
Swelling caused by fluid buildup in body tissues.
Internal examination using a thin camera tube, not imaging.
A medical check-up or test, not a written assessment.
A medical check-up or test, not an assessment or inspection.
Extreme physical or mental tiredness, not running out.
To lose consciousness briefly, not to be weak or dim.
Extreme tiredness or weakness, not a material breaking down.
A sudden seizure or convulsion, not suitable clothing.
A parasite like athlete's foot; not the edible mushroom.
Enlarged thyroid gland in the neck.
A painful joint disease from uric acid buildup.
The tissue around teeth, not adhesive.
Severe bleeding inside or outside the body.
Swollen veins around the anus; internal or external.
Organ pushes through a weak muscle wall.
Viral infection causing painful blisters on skin or mucous membranes.
Itchy raised skin welts from allergic reaction.
Rough or raspy voice quality.
Abnormally high blood pressure.
Dangerously low body temperature from cold exposure.
A device surgically placed inside the body, not simply inserted.
Male inability to achieve or maintain erection.
A clean cut made by surgical knife.
Loss of bladder or bowel control.
Uncomfortable stomach distress after eating.
Swelling, redness, heat, and pain as body's response to injury.
Severe flu infection, worse than a common cold.
Breathing in; the act of drawing air into lungs.
Medicine given by needle piercing the skin.
Vaccine introduction to build immunity.
Poisoning by a toxic substance, not drunkenness.
A disease (tetanus) causing jaw stiffness, not actual jaw locking.
Sudden and severe (of illness), not just sharp or pointed.
Relating to body fat tissue, not oil or grease in general.
Unfavorable (effect/reaction), not just opposing or against.
A thick, greasy healing paste — not a thin liquid cream.
A soft cosmetic or medical preparation — not whipped cream to eat.
A small solid medication to swallow — not a computer device.
Thick sweet liquid medicine, not the kind poured on pancakes.
To watch or track progress — or the device displaying vital signs.
Essential to life — used for vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure).
A measurable medical indicator (like temperature) — not a written notice.
A group of symptoms appearing together — not a single disease.
Loss of normal function, often psychological — not just untidiness.
A medical state or illness — not a requirement or circumstance.
Long-lasting or recurring — not necessarily severe.
Short-term or lasting only a brief time — opposite of chronic.
The immune system attacks the body's own tissues.
Determined by genes — may not run in families (new mutation).
Passed down from parents to children through genes.
Forced separation to prevent spread — from a place or source.
Separation from others — often for an infected person.
Protected against a disease — usually from vaccination or past infection.
Excessive body fat — a medical condition, not just overweight.
A doctor who performs operations — not all doctors are surgeons.
A person receiving medical care — not the virtue of being tolerant.
Bad breath, usually from medical or dental issues.
Extreme fatigue and lack of energy — deeper than just tiredness.
A device that converts liquid medicine into a fine mist to breathe in.
A drug that prevents blood clotting — used to stop thrombosis.
A drug that blocks histamine — relieves allergic reactions.
The main artery carrying blood from the heart.
Temporary stop in breathing during sleep — not permanent.
Inflammation of the appendix — a surgical emergency.
Desire to eat — not the food itself.
Irregular heartbeat — may be harmless or serious.
Breathing in food or liquid by accident — can be dangerous.
Having no symptoms — the person feels fine but may be infected.
Wasting away of muscle or organ tissue from disuse.
Listening to internal body sounds with a stethoscope.
Affecting both sides of the body equally.
A yellowish waste product from broken-down red blood cells.
A mental disorder with extreme mood swings — not everyday mood changes.
Complete or near-complete loss of vision — partial sight is low vision.
Uneven patches of colour or rash — irregular appearance.
A lump or rounded mass — often medicine in pill form or food in throat.
Fluid-filled blisters on the skin, not simple bumps.
A fluid-filled sac near joints, not a general pouch.
Severe wasting and weight loss from illness, not normal thinness.
Hardened skin from pressure; also bone repair tissue—context determines which.
A fungus; the yeast infection it causes, not bacteria.
Medical treatment and support, not just general concern.
Someone who has a disease gene or infection but may show no symptoms.
One instance of a disease or patient, not a container.
A person injured or killed in an accident or disaster.
Clouding of the eye lens; not a waterfall despite the similar word.
Inflammation of mucous membranes causing discharge, especially in the nose.
Relating to the tail end or lower body, not the head.
Formation of air-filled holes in tissue or lung from disease.
Material used to bond dental fillings or coat tooth roots.
The main body of a vertebra, not a general centre.
Relating to the cheek or the inner cheek surface.
A cavity or hollow space, same as cavitas or cavity.
